basis: wet mass fraction; mass fractions sum to 1
mass_balance_method: VARTA measured dry matter plus published dry-basis component estimates converted to wet basis. The 7.2% DM Smit roadside-grass extractive-sugar aggregate is partitioned using normalized midpoints of reported Italian ryegrass glucose, fructose, sucrose, and fructosan ranges; this cross-study allocation is class C and preserves the aggregate sugar mass. Starch uses the 34 g/kg DM mean reported by Gierus et al. (2024) for a cultivated perennial-ryegrass NIRS calibration/validation set, scaled using the measured VARTA dry-matter fraction; it is a class-C cross-material proxy, not a roadside-grass or GreenHub-batch assay. The reported 1–169 g/kg DM range is not a probability distribution, and the NIRS R² is 0.77. A low-transferability literature nitrate-N result is converted to nitrate-ion mass using the molecular-weight ratio and the VARTA dry-matter fraction. VARTA measured chloride is represented as chloride ion and separated from the total-ash proxy. Summer roadside-grass Cr, Ni, Cd, Hg, and Pb are summed as a low-transferability contaminant proxy and also deducted from the total-ash proxy to avoid counting these species twice. A low-transferability grass pesticide-residue proxy is calculated from detected residue count and mean detected concentration, with non-detections treated as zero; this is a lower-bound literature proxy, not a VARTA measurement. A PFAS proxy uses the mean of three reported orchard-grass control replicate sums (non-detects treated as zero) and the VARTA dry-matter fraction; it is class C and is not a Dutch roadside-grass assay. Acetic acid uses the untreated landscape-grass value reported by Heller et al. (2023), converted from g/kg fresh matter to kg/kg wet feed; this is a class-C cross-context proxy, not a VARTA measurement. The net closure difference is assigned to ParticulateBiodegradableOrganics; this residual is an unmeasured allocation, not a measured component speciation. The ParticulateBiodegradableOrganics value is the calculated closure residual (1 minus all other stored wet-mass fractions) for this authored profile only; it is not a measured or chemically identified pool and must be recomputed when any component changes. Unmeasured nonzero legacy fractions remain compatibility fallbacks, not evidence of presence or absence.

source.basis: Smit et al. 2022 supports 10.7 g total protein/100 g dry roadside grass. For this protein partition, Hoekstra et al. 2008 reports mean ryegrass true-protein N fractions of 175 g/kg total N as buffer-soluble B1N and 592 g/kg total N as non-soluble protein-associated fractions (B2N+B3N+CN). The source label B1N is distinct from BIN, the buffer-insoluble nitrogen assay. Their normalized ratio 175/(175+592) is transferred as a GreenHub-specific class-C split; it is not a GreenHub assay or industrial juice-recovery measurement.
source.partition_assumption: Soluble share = 175/(175+592) = 0.2281616688 from the mean Hoekstra lamina/sheath N fractions; non-soluble share = 0.7718383312. The normalized share is applied to Smit's total protein and converted using the measured VARTA dry-matter fraction. Both pseudo-components use the same 16% N convention. Not measured in GreenHub.
source.uncertainty: Transfer uncertainty is not quantified. Hoekstra reports tissue means varying by lamina/sheath and the experiment varied season, nitrogen rate, cultivar, regrowth period, and cutting height. Buffer solubility is only a proxy for the GreenHub model's soluble/suspended distinction.

source.source: Residual of the Smit roadside-grass extractive-sugar aggregate after literature-proxy allocation to free monosaccharides
source.source_title: Biomass Pre-Extraction as a Versatile Strategy to Improve Biorefinery Feedstock Flexibility, Sugar Yields, and Lignin Purity
source.source_location: Smit et al. main-text discussion accompanying Figure 2; Masaki & Ohyama (1976), J-STAGE abstract
source.geography: Study geography not verified in the available source metadata
source.basis: Smit et al. reports a 0.072 kg extractive-sugar pool/kg dry roadside grass. Masaki & Ohyama report component ranges for Italian ryegrass; the normalized range midpoints are used only as allocation weights. EntrappedSugars is the remaining aggregate pool after glucose, fructose, and sucrose are allocated.
source.conversion_method: For source-reported ranges glucose 1.0–4.4, fructose 0.7–5.0, sucrose 0.3–4.5, and fructosan 1.2–12.6 % DM: calculate midpoints (2.7, 2.85, 2.4, 6.9), normalize by 14.85, multiply each share by 0.072 kg/kg DM and VARTA DM fraction 0.143. EntrappedSugars is the fructosan-weight remainder; total allocated sugars remain 0.072 kg/kg DM.
source.uncertainty: The source ranges span growth stages and aftermaths but are not means or probability bounds. The range-midpoint ratios are a modelling allocation transferred from cultivated Italian ryegrass to roadside grass; no same-sample free-sugar assay or allocation uncertainty distribution is available.
source.applicability: Class-C GreenHub proxy combining a roadside-grass aggregate with cultivated Italian ryegrass species ratios; not a species-resolved VARTA measurement. Sensitivity should use the published component ranges and matched assays should replace it.

source.geography: Greenhouse experiment at Penn State University Park, Pennsylvania, USA; orchard grass (Dactylis glomerata); control soil and tap-water treatment.
source.basis: Mean sum of the reported concentrations of targeted PFAS in the three control first-cutting orchard-grass replicates, with table non-detects treated as zero. This is a lower-bound aggregate of 40 targeted analytes, not a measurement of all persistent organics.
source.conversion_method: mean(4.595, 1.824, 1.054) µg/kg dry × GreenHub VARTA dry_matter_fraction 0.143 × 1e-9 kg/µg = 3.56213e-10 kg targeted PFAS/kg GreenHub wet-feed proxy.
source.uncertainty: Only three composite subsamples from one greenhouse control treatment and one harvest were reported; they are not three independent roadside sites. Non-detects treated as zero bias the total downward. Unmeasured PFAS, precursors, extraction recoveries, and Dutch roadside transfer are not quantified.
source.license: Source article is CC BY-NC 4.0; this is a cited derived summary, not a redistribution of the article or its full raw dataset.
source.applicability: Class C transfer proxy for the model's PFAS-only PersistentOrganics pool. Not Dutch roadside grass, not a VARTA assay, not a compliance result, and not a claim that PFAS are absent. Replace with matched, analyte-resolved assays on incoming grass and separated process fractions.

source.source_evidence_class: Primary grass-residue monitoring; GreenHub application is a transfer-limited proxy.
source.source: Prechsl et al. 2022, grass pesticide-residue monitoring in South Tyrol
source.source_title: Long-term monitoring of pesticide residues on public sites: A regional approach to survey and reduce spray drift
source.source_location: Results, section 3.1; study summary: 399 grass sample analyses, 334 detections, mean concentration 0.0645 mg/kg fresh weight over detected residues; LOQ 0.01 mg/kg.
source.geography: Public grass sites in South Tyrol, Northern Italy; 2018–2021; selected sites include sensitive zones near orchards and vineyards.
source.basis: Lower-bound estimated mean summed pesticide-residue mass per analyzed fresh-grass sample, calculated from the reported number of detections and mean concentration among detections. Non-detections and concentrations below the limit of quantification are treated as zero for this calculation; this does not establish absence.
source.conversion_method: (0.0645 mg/kg fresh grass × 334 detections ÷ 399 analyzed samples) × 1e-6 kg/mg = 5.3992481203007515e-8 kg pesticide residue/kg wet grass.
source.uncertainty: The paper reports variability across detected residues, not the distribution of total residue mass per sample. Treating non-detections and below-LOQ concentrations as zero makes the derived mean a lower bound. Transfer uncertainty to Dutch roadside grass is unquantified.
source.applicability: Class C proxy for the aggregate pesticide pool only. South Tyrol public-site grass is not Dutch roadside biomass, and selected sites were influenced by local agricultural spray drift. Not a compliance or safety assessment; replace with a matched GreenHub contaminant panel when available.

source.source: Della Rosa et al. 2022, Table 1, FR0 (100% cultivated perennial ryegrass); low-transferability literature nitrate-N proxy
source.source_title: Substituting ryegrass-based pasture with graded levels of forage rape in the diet of lambs decreases methane emissions and increases propionate, succinate, and primary alcohols in the rumen
source.source_location: Table 1, FR0 (100% ryegrass) column, printed p. 3; nitrate-N row
source.geography: AgResearch Aorangi Farm, Palmerston North, New Zealand
source.basis: The source reports 618 ± 155 mg nitrate-N/kg dry matter. Applying the separate VARTA sample's measured dry-matter fraction (0.143) and converting N mass to nitrate-ion mass gives 0.3912 ± 0.0981 g NO3-/kg wet feed. This is a cross-source literature assumption, not a measurement of the VARTA sample.
source.conversion_method: 618 mg nitrate-N/kg DM × 0.143 kg DM/kg wet × (62.0049 g/mol NO3- ÷ 14.0067 g/mol N) × 1e-6 kg/mg = 0.0003912143 kg NO3-/kg wet feed. The reported within-study SD converts to 0.0000981201 kg/kg wet feed.
source.uncertainty: The source SD is 155 mg nitrate-N/kg DM; composition-table replicate count is not stated. Converted within-study SD is reported, but transfer uncertainty from cultivated New Zealand ryegrass to GreenHub roadside/VARTA grass is unquantified and not propagated.
source.applicability: C-class proxy for nitrate ion only. The source measures nitrate-N in cultivated ryegrass, not nitrate in GreenHub roadside grass; this estimate does not derive from or reconcile the VARTA total-N measurement.

source.source: Project-supplied VARTA whole-grass laboratory result
source.source_location: Nutriënten Vezel, row 7, sample 3 (Greenhub whole grass), chloride result

source.basis: The source reports chloride at 330 mmol/kg dry matter and 11.7 g/kg dry matter. The analyte is mapped to the model chloride-anion pool for the same sample; the laboratory extraction method and replicate uncertainty were not supplied.
source.conversion_method: 11.7 g chloride/kg dry matter × 0.143 kg dry matter/kg wet feed ÷ 1000 g/kg = 0.0016731 kg Cl−/kg wet feed

source.applicability: Directly applicable to the GreenHub whole-grass sample represented by the UI default. Do not inherit as another project's default.

source.source: Brown et al. 2020
source.source_title: An Assessment of Road-Verge Grass as a Feedstock for Farm-Fed Anaerobic Digestion Plants
source.source_location: Table 3; fresh verge grass, proximate analysis on dry basis
source.geography: United Kingdom; precise sample location not recorded in this profile
source.basis: Brown et al. reports total ash of 17.9% dry matter for fresh verge grass. The model separates the VARTA measured chloride analyte and the Czubaszek summer potentially-toxic-element proxy from this total-ash pool for component mass bookkeeping.
source.conversion_method: (0.179 kg total ash/kg dry matter − 0.0117 kg chloride/kg dry matter − 0.00001297 kg/kg dry matter potentially-toxic elements) × VARTA dry-matter fraction 0.143 = 0.02392204529 kg residual ash pool/kg wet feed
source.uncertainty: Brown et al. reports 17.9 ± 2.0% dry matter; VARTA chloride is measured on another sample basis with no assay uncertainty reported; Czubaszek et al. reports analyte-specific SDs for a different roadside-grass sample. Covariance, ash-method chloride retention, and cross-study transfer uncertainty are unknown; central values only are used.
source.applicability: Mixed-evidence bookkeeping pool for GreenHub's July VARTA sample. It is not a measured VARTA ash result; chloride retention during ashing is unknown, and the full inorganic-ion mass/charge balance is not resolved.

source.source: Czubaszek et al. 2023, summer roadside-grass Table 4; proxy scaled to the VARTA dry-matter fraction
source.source_evidence_class: Primary experimental literature measurements; GreenHub application is C-class because of cross-study and geographic transfer.
source.source_title: Grass from Road Verges as a Substrate for Biogas Production
source.authors: R. Czubaszek; A. Wysocka-Czubaszek; G. Zając; et al.
source.source_location: Table 4, p. 8; summer 2019 cutting; reported on dry matter
source.geography: Urban road verges and median strips, Białystok, northeastern Poland
source.basis: Sum of the reported summer Cr, Ni, Cd, Hg, and Pb means (12.97 mg/kg dry matter), multiplied by the VARTA sample's measured dry-matter fraction. This is a literature proxy, not a measurement of the VARTA sample.
source.conversion_method: (7.54 + 0.78 + 0.27 + 1.93 + 2.45) mg/kg dry matter × 0.143 kg dry matter/kg wet feed × 1e-6 kg/mg = 1.85471e-6 kg/kg wet feed
source.uncertainty: Source reports analyte-specific SDs from triplicate laboratory analyses, not independent field sites. Aggregate covariance and transfer uncertainty are unknown; SDs are not combined. Arsenic is not included because this source table does not report it.
source.applicability: Summer roadside-grass comparator for GreenHub's July sample, but collected in Białystok, Poland in 2019. Not a Dutch contaminant assay and not evidence of regulatory or product compliance.
